summary: Mobility is stabilising near pre‑pandemic levels, but public transport ridership remains 24% below 2019 and fuel savings, while substantial, are only 42% of the MCO peak. High‑risk sectors are moving freely, creating equity and congestion concerns that require focused policy action.

signals.detail: Weekly fuel savings of 35.7 million litres represent 42% of the MCO peak, reflecting the effectiveness of high fuel prices and the ongoing WFH regime. Continued price signals can further curb consumption, but the gap to pre‑pandemic savings suggests additional demand‑side measures are needed.

Daily PT trips total 1.09 million, roughly 24% below the 2019 average of 1.43 million, indicating a lag in modal recovery despite a ridership component of 76.1. Without targeted incentives, the shortfall risks entrenching private‑vehicle dependence.

Retail & Services, Logistics and Construction show mobility scores of 85‑95 and are flagged HIGH risk, signalling robust economic activity but also heightened exposure to fuel price volatility and congestion externalities. Monitoring these sectors is critical for macro‑stability.

WFH adoption varies sharply: 60% in Public & GLCs versus 5‑15% in high‑mobility sectors, creating uneven pressure on transport networks. Aligning remote‑work incentives across sectors would distribute mobility benefits more evenly.

High fuel prices have not translated into a PT rebound; instead, private vehicle use remains strong in high‑risk sectors, risking a durable shift away from sustainable modes. Strategic investments in integrated, affordable PT are required to reverse this trend.

recommendation: Introduce a tiered PT fare subsidy to lift daily ridership to 1.3 million trips by end‑2027, coupled with a 10% reduction target in weekly fuel consumption through a capped fuel price and expanded EV charging infrastructure. Extend WFH incentives to Logistics, Retail and Construction to lower peak‑hour traffic and improve equity across sectors.
